sections.title: Acids & Bases: Theories and Strength
sections.subtitle: Complete Lesson Pack · Brønsted–Lowry · pH & pOH · Acid Strength

sections.title: Learning Objectives
items: Identify Brønsted–Lowry acids, bases, and conjugate acid–base pairs
Write equations for acid and base ionization reactions
Use the ion-product constant for water (Kw) to find [H3O+] and [OH−]
Convert between pH, pOH, [H3O+], and [OH−] at 25 °C
Compare acid strength using Ka and percent ionization
Describe the acid–base behavior of amphiprotic species

sections.title: Concept 1 — Defining Acids & Bases (Brønsted–Lowry)
body: An acid is any species that donates a proton (H+) to another species; a base is any species that accepts a proton. This is the Brønsted–Lowry definition, and it is more general than the Arrhenius definition (which requires the production of H3O+ or OH− in water).

In any Brønsted–Lowry reaction, two conjugate pairs are present: when an acid donates a proton, the remaining species is its conjugate base; when a base accepts a proton, the product is its conjugate acid.
Example: In the reaction NH3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq), water donates a proton to ammonia. Water is the acid and its conjugate base is OH−; ammonia is the base and its conjugate acid is NH4+.
Amphiprotic species (such as H2O, HCO3−, and HSO4−) can either donate or accept a proton depending on the other reactant.

worked_example.question: Label the acid, base, conjugate acid, and conjugate base in the reaction: HCN(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ CN−(aq) + H3O+(aq)
worked_example.solution: HCN donates a proton to water: HCN is the acid and CN− is its conjugate base. H2O accepts the proton: water is the base and H3O+ is its conjugate acid.

common_mistakes: Confusing 'conjugate' with 'concentration' — a conjugate pair differs by exactly one proton (H+).
Forgetting that H3O+ (hydronium) is the form H+ takes in water.

sections.title: Concept 2 — Water Autoionization and the Ion-Product Constant (Kw)
body: Water autoionizes to a tiny extent: H2O(l) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + OH−(aq).
At 25 °C, the ion-product constant is Kw = [H3O+][OH−] = 1.0 × 10−14.
In pure water, [H3O+] = [OH−] = 1.0 × 10−7 M. Kw increases with temperature because autoionization is endothermic (Kw ≈ 5.6 × 10−13 at 100 °C).

worked_example.question: At 25 °C, a solution has [OH−] = 2.5 × 10−4 M. Find [H3O+] and decide if the solution is acidic, basic, or neutral.

common_mistakes: Using Kw = 1.0 × 10−14 at temperatures other than 25 °C.
Multiplying instead of dividing when solving for a missing ion concentration.

sections.title: Concept 3 — pH, pOH, and the pH Scale
body: pH = −log[H3O+] and pOH = −log[OH−]. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.00 for any aqueous solution.
Acidic solutions: [H3O+] > 1.0 × 10−7 M and pH < 7. Basic: [H3O+] < 1.0 × 10−7 M and pH > 7. Neutral: pH = 7 at 25 °C.
A one-unit pH change corresponds to a tenfold change in [H3O+].

worked_example.question: What are the pH and pOH of a 0.010 M solution of HCl (a strong acid that ionizes completely)?

common_mistakes: Forgetting the minus sign: pH = −log[H3O+], not log[H3O+].
Assuming pH = 7 is neutral at all temperatures (it is only true at 25 °C).

sections.title: Concept 4 — Relative Strengths of Acids and Bases
body: Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4) ionize completely in water. Weak acids (HF, CH3COOH, HCN, HNO2) ionize only partially.
The strength of a weak acid is quantified by its ionization constant Ka: the larger Ka, the stronger the acid. For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = Kw.
Water has a leveling effect: in water, the strongest acid possible is H3O+ and the strongest base possible is OH−. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
Binary acid strength increases left to right across a period (CH4 < NH3 < H2O < HF) and down a group (HF < HCl < HBr < HI).

worked_example.question: For HF (Ka = 6.8 × 10−4) and HCN (Ka = 6.2 × 10−10), which is the stronger acid, and which is the stronger conjugate base?
worked_example.solution: HF has the larger Ka, so HF is the stronger acid and CN− is the stronger conjugate base (the weaker acid has the stronger conjugate base).

common_mistakes: Thinking 'strong' means 'concentrated' — strength depends on Ka (extent of ionization), not concentration.
Assuming all acids with H in the formula are strong.

items.q: Write an equation showing water acting as a Brønsted–Lowry acid when it reacts with ammonia, NH3.
Write an equation showing water acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base when it reacts with hydrogen cyanide, HCN.
For each species, write the formula of its conjugate base: (a) H2O (b) NH4+ (c) HSO4− (d) H2CO3
For each species, write the formula of its conjugate acid: (a) OH− (b) NH3 (c) CO32− (d) H2PO4−
In the reaction HSO4−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ SO42−(aq) + H3O+(aq), identify the acid, base, conjugate acid, and conjugate base.
items.answer: Acid: HSO4− · Base: H2O · Conjugate acid: H3O+ · Conjugate base: SO42−

items.q: Which of the following species are amphiprotic? H2O, OH−, HCO3−, NH4+, HSO4−
items.answer: H2O, HCO3−, and HSO4− (each can donate OR accept a proton; OH− can only accept and NH4+ can only donate)
items.explain: Amphiprotic species must have at least one H to donate and be able to accept another H+. OH− has no H to donate; NH4+ has no lone pair to accept a proton easily in water.

items.q: Write the two possible reactions of the amphiprotic ion HCO3−: (a) as an acid with water (b) as a base with water.
items.answer: (a) HCO3−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ CO32−(aq) + H3O+(aq) (b) HCO3−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H2CO3(aq) + OH−(aq)

items.q: Is the autoionization of water endothermic or exothermic? Explain using the values Kw = 2.9 × 10−14 at 40 °C and Kw = 9.3 × 10−14 at 60 °C.
items.answer: Endothermic — Kw increases with temperature, so heat is absorbed (an endothermic process shifts toward products when temperature rises).

sections.title: Part B — Kw, pH, and pOH Calculations (Questions 9–16)

items.q: Calculate [H3O+] and [OH−] in pure water at 25 °C.
A solution at 25 °C has [H3O+] = 3.2 × 10−5 M. Calculate [OH−]. Is the solution acidic, basic, or neutral?
Calculate the pH and pOH of a 0.035 M solution of HNO3, which ionizes completely.
Calculate the pH and pOH of a 0.0042 M solution of KOH, which ionizes completely.
What are [H3O+] and [OH−] in a solution whose pH is 4.20?
The [H3O+] in a sample of rainwater is 1.7 × 10−6 M at 25 °C. What is the concentration of hydroxide ions?
The [OH−] in household ammonia is 3.2 × 10−3 M at 25 °C. What is [H3O+] and the pH?
A solution has pH = 9.35. Calculate pOH, [H3O+], and [OH−]. Classify the solution.
Arrange the following in order of increasing acid strength: HF, HCl, HBr, HI. Explain the trend.
items.answer: HF < HCl < HBr < HI. Down group 17, the H–X bond weakens (bond enthalpy decreases), so ionization is easier.

items.q: Given Ka values: CH3COOH (1.8 × 10−5), HF (6.8 × 10−4), HCN (6.2 × 10−10). Rank the acids from weakest to strongest.
items.answer: HCN < CH3COOH < HF (smaller Ka = weaker acid)

items.q: For the conjugate pair HCN/CN−, Ka(HCN) = 6.2 × 10−10. Calculate Kb for CN−.
A 0.10 M solution of a weak acid HA is 2.4% ionized. Calculate [H3O+] and Ka.
The pH of a 0.23 M solution of HF is 1.92. Determine Ka for HF.
Explain why 'strong acid' does not mean 'concentrated acid.' Give an example of a dilute solution of a strong acid and a concentrated solution of a weak acid.
items.answer: Strength = extent of ionization (Ka); concentration = amount of solute per liter. A 0.0001 M HCl (strong, dilute) has lower [H3O+] than 6 M CH3COOH (weak, concentrated) even though HCl ionizes completely.

sections.title: Key Terms
items: acid
A species that donates a proton (H+) in a Brønsted–Lowry reaction
base
A species that accepts a proton (H+) in a Brønsted–Lowry reaction
conjugate acid
The species formed when a base accepts a proton
conjugate base
The species remaining after an acid donates a proton
amphiprotic
Able to act as either a proton donor or a proton acceptor
autoionization
Reaction of identical molecules to produce ions (e.g., water producing H3O+ and OH−)
ion-product constant (Kw)
pH
−log[H3O+], a measure of hydronium ion concentration
pOH
−log[OH−], a measure of hydroxide ion concentration
ionization constant (Ka)
Equilibrium constant for the ionization of a weak acid; larger Ka = stronger acid
